This is a HUGE point for any hedge fund investor and trader (when assessing a return stream). 

I’ve seen this across a few exceptional funds. A strategy might have a historical CAGR of 15% with a maximum drawdown of just 5%. Excellent numbers on paper. But investors don’t all enter on the first day of that track record.

Suppose you invest when the fund is already up 15% for the year. The next four monthly returns are -1%, -1.5%, -1%, and -1.5%.

Your experience is now a roughly 5% loss. You participated in none of the gains that preceded it, but all of the subsequent drawdown.

Almost immediately, regret can set in. You question the allocation, the manager, and the process, even though those losses could reflect ordinary variance within the strategy rather than any deterioration in its edge. It’s a psychological phenomenon that overtakes even some experienced investors. It’s never a good feeling to see losses when you deploy capital towards a strategy. 

But this is something that’s important to distinguish early on and that only comes from truly understanding the process and potential distribution. If you don’t, you’ll just end up becoming a return chaser that crab trades / invests their way into suboptimal returns. 

Process before everything and the rest will take care of itself.

4 data leaks reported today:

1. Coinbase's vendor Amplitude exposed some users’ contact data (funds unaffected).
2. Bithumb (Korea) had user data leaks.

In TradFi, two securities firms in Korea leaked data: 
3. Mirae Asset
4. Daishin Securities

You can't prevent a leak, but you can protect yourself.

Leaked exchange data (names, emails, phone numbers, addresses, ID documents, transaction history) is mostly used for phishing, SIM swapping, and social engineering.

Reduce info you share
- Use a unique email alias for each exchange (SimpleLogin, Apple Hide My Email, etc). A leak then can't be linked to your other accounts, and you can spot which service leaked.
- Share only what's required. Don't add optional profile details.
- Use a dedicated phone number (a VoIP or secondary SIM) for exchange accounts if you can, since leaked numbers are the main route to SIM swaps.

Lock down the account
- Use a unique, long password from a password manager.
- Turn on hardware security keys (YubiKey) or passkeys, or at least an authenticator app.
- Avoid SMS 2FA.
- Enable withdrawal address whitelisting and a withdrawal time lock if the exchange offers them.
- Set up an anti-phishing code, which puts a code you choose in every legitimate email from the exchange.
- Review active sessions and API keys regularly. Delete any API keys you don't use.
- Restrict API keys to withdraw-disabled and IP-whitelisted.

Defend against
- SIM swapping: Ask your carrier to add a port-out PIN or number lock.
- Phishing and impersonation: Assume anyone who contacts you about your account, "security issues," or "refund recovery" is a scammer, even if they know your name, balance, or recent trades.
- Exchange support staff don't ask for your password, 2FA codes, or seed phrase.
- Never click links in emails or texts. Go to the site yourself.

- "Wrench attacks": Leaked addresses plus holdings data have led to real-world extortion and robberies. Don't publicize your holdings, and keep large balances out of anything tied to your home address if you can.

If a breach is announced
1. Change the exchange password and any other account that reused it.
2. Check http://haveibeenpwned.com for your email address.
3. Revoke API keys and active sessions.
4. Review recent withdrawals and security settings.
5. Watch for phishing emails and texts that reference the breach, because scammers move fast after one.

Stay SAFU! 🙏

Cliff Sosin on how frontier intelligence gets commoditized:

"You start out with very inadequate models that are basically able to do a very small subset of jobs. The models get better, and they work their way up the stack. 

With each successive step up, the frontier model has unlocked a larger addressable market.

But you would never use a frontier model for a chatbot in a customer service application. You'd be an idiot. Those areas, they clearly commoditize. 

There's this wave of hard tasks where you really need a frontier model, and then behind that, you don’t.

The bull story would be, 'People will pay anything for a model that can figure out how to cure cancer.' Maybe that's true. 

But I think figuring out how to cure cancer requires touching reality, and I’m not sure that more IQ gets you that.

It’s like this diamond-shaped demand frontier, where initially, you get wider and wider uses, and then it starts to get more and more rarefied. How often do you really need a 300 IQ?

It strikes me as totally reasonable that there are very few use cases for super elite intelligence. There are lots of use cases for very good intelligence. That very good intelligence is highly competitive and commoditized.

If good enough intelligence is very, very cheap, then how much good enough intelligence are people gonna buy?"

posts.text:
Five initial remarks on the dramatic election results in Israel. All based on exit polls and might change.

1. Don’t let the noise distract you. Netanyahu has just lost this election, and resoundingly.

The numbers tell the story. His current coalition holds 68 seats in the Knesset. According to the exit polls, that same bloc is projected to win between 50 and 53 seats. Again, exit polls are only exit polls. But if these numbers hold, this represents a decline of more than 20% in the parliamentary strength of the Netanyahu bloc. A substantial defeat.

2. The most significant change is the turnout of Arab voters.

Possibly for the first time in Israel’s history, turnout among Arab citizens of Israel was as high as among Jewish voters- and according to some estimates, it may actually be higher. Not far from 80% turnout. Gone are the days in which Israeli Arabs wanted to boycott the election as a protest against the state legitimacy. 

Across Jewish public in Israel, turnout is also approaching 80%. Israelis came out to vote in massive numbers, determined to influence the future of their country.

The reason Arab voters turned out in such extraordinary numbers was not primarily Gaza or Palestinian statehood- issues that alway dominated the local Arab discourse. It was their rights as citizens of Israel, a deep sense of discrimination by the far-right Netanyahu government, and specifically the conduct of Itamar Ben-Gvir, the minister responsible for the police. Ben-Gvir, who has been convicted of incitement to racism and supporting a terrorist organization, is a disciple of Meir Kahane’s ideology of Jewish supremacy. Under his watch, crime in Arab communities and cities has been neglected.

Arab citizens responded with a remarkable mobilization at the ballot box, seeking to help remove this government from power.

3. Netanyahu has lost. But has Eisenkot won?
Gadi Eisenkot, exactly as the polls suggested, is emerging as the leading candidate to form the next government. Israel’s president will probably give him the mandate to try to assemble a coalition.

 However, according to the same exit polls- and the final results could change things for better or worse- Eisenkot does not have the numbers to form a stable, coherent, and politically homogeneous coalition.

This is the essential distinction: Netanyahu has lost the election. But it is not yet clear that Eisenkot has won it. That will only become clear if he can actually form a government. It could be a minority government supported by Arab parties, probably from outside the coalition; an arrangement with Likud, with or without Netanyahu; or some other combination of parties.

Right now, the road ahead looks extremely difficult. Eisenkot does not have the 61 seats needed for a cohesive, centrist, Zionist coalition.

The right-wing parties in the bloc seeking change will not sit in a government alongside Arab parties that support Palestinian statehood, and some are reluctant even to rely on their support from outside. Eisenkot has also essentially ruled out governing with the ultra-Orthodox parties, because of his position on military conscription.

Taken together, these constraints make it extremely difficult for him to translate his electoral achievement into an actual government. He may have to compromise on some of his principles- or risk sending Israel into another election.

4. What actually happened to Netanyahu?

The only silver lining for the prime minister at the moment is that Likud appears to have emerged as the largest party in the Knesset. This is also a surprise compared with the polls, which suggested that Likud would win significantly fewer seats.

But the real story is the breakdown within the Netanyahu bloc. What happened is that Likud essentially cannibalized its own bloc, drawing voters away from far-right parties and some of the ultra-Orthodox parties, back to Likud itself.

posts.text:
Cliff Sosin on the limits of intelligence:

"Superintelligence arrived. You probably didn't notice, because it turned out to be kind of incremental.

I think we overrated intelligence, or misread what it is. 

We hold a thin scatter of facts about the world, and intelligence or reasoning is whatever fills the space between them.

Where the space between the facts behaves well, this is close to godlike. Most of what matters doesn't behave like that. 

The universe is mostly the emergent behavior of complex systems. Stir cream into coffee. Watch a storm build out of nothing but atmospheric temperature differences and water vapor. 

You have to run the thing.

The takeoff story assumed the limit was thinking. It isn't. The limit is contact with reality. 

A smarter reasoner fills the gaps between known facts in simple areas faster and better, but it doesn’t produce new facts.

An AI will hand you a genuinely clever design for a jet turbine blade. It might be far more likely to work than anything your engineers came up with. 

It'll still probably fail, because that’s the base rate at the edge of what anyone knows. The only way to find out is to build the blade and try to break it.

That's the real limit on learning, and it doesn't care how smart you are. Coming up with ideas was never the hard part. The hard part is how fast reality answers them.

Most problems can't be worked out at a desk by thinking. Those stay bound by how fast we can build the thing and see if it holds, and that clock barely moves."

From his essay "Maybe Intelligence Ain't All That." He walks through it here.

posts.name: Patrick OShaughnessy
posts.text:
Cliff Sosin on why you want to own the complements to cheap intelligence, like Meta does:

"I've found it helpful to assume everyone has really great intelligence and ask what's left. 

If intelligence becomes cheap and ubiquitous, what you want to own are the complements to intelligence. 

The complements are data, attention, love, physical proximity, scale, regulatory capture.

Let's talk about Meta. They have $250 billion of revenue, and they spend $250 billion a year. The question you might ask is, what do they spend it on? A really reductionist view is that they spend it all on intelligence.

They're buying data centers. They're literally buying inference. They're paying really smart people to write algorithms. They're writing code. That's just intelligence.

If you think forward with the fact that the price of intelligence is falling by a factor of a hundred or something over the next five years, their costs kind of go away.

Maybe instead of taking their cost to zero with much better intelligence at much lower prices, maybe they can sell a few more ads.

All of this is downstream of what they possess, which is not destroyed by ubiquitous intelligence, which is data and attention. 

I don't think that the availability of cheap and ubiquitous intelligence is gonna cause people not to be interested in watching funny 20-second videos."

posts.name: Meb Faber
posts.text:
Should we make a modern version?

Via @Sothebys 

Catalogue Note

This rare deck of playing cards, published soon after the South Sea Bubble stock market collapse, features a series of illustrations that satirize the recent stock market madness and the various "bubble" companies that duped gullible investors into buying worthless shares.

In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, there was a vogue for playing cards that featured elaborate, themed designs, in addition to suits and ranks. The small-sized engravings on the card faces could include imagery from a variety of sources, ranging from geography, to literature, and history. This gave the cards a somewhat disparate twofold purpose — entertainment and education.

The All the Bubbles deck was inspired by current events, namely the dubious stock market schemes that were created in the midst of the Mississippi Bubble and the South Sea Bubble crashes. These "bubbles" are often thought of as the world's first major stock market crashes. The Mississippi Bubble, a French stock market crash, was orchestrated by the Scottish economist John Law, whose Mississippi Company held a monopoly on trade between France and its colonies. After the Company started selling shares to investors, it became the subject of rampant speculation. The resulting investment mania reached all levels of society, from servants to the aristocracy. In 1720, the bubble burst, wiping out investors and sending the French economy into a period of massive inflation. The South Sea Bubble, which occurred the same year in England, was a parallel stock market crash involving shares in the South Sea Company.

Bowles' deck illustrates a variety of other risky stock market ventures that were open to investors, many of which had emerged during the South Sea Bubble mania. The companies' offerings range from the precarious to the absurd, and are ridiculed here as attempts to exploit the public's blind desire to get rich quickly. The cards feature an array of ephemeral "bubble" stock companies, both real and imagined, including the Pennsylvania Company, life, ship, and horse insurance companies, and various commodities investments, ranging from copper and brass, to rock salt and radish oil. These types of companies would soon be regulated in Parliament by the Bubble Act of 1720, which required all joint-stock companies to have a royal charter in order to issue shares.

Is China hiding its true exposure to US Treasuries?

China’s Treasury holdings fell -$27 billion in August, to $591 billion, their lowest level since August 2008.

At the same time, Canada’s holdings of US Treasuries jumped +$38 billion in August, to $465 billion, their 3rd-highest on record.

Since the beginning of 2019, Canada’s holdings have surged +$369 billion, or +384%, while China’s have declined -$534 billion, or -48%.

This divergence may partly reflect China moving its US securities to foreign custodians, making its actual exposure to American debt appear smaller and creating the impression of faster financial decoupling from the US Dollar.

Meanwhile, Belgium and Luxembourg, widely believed to hold some Chinese Treasury assets through custodial accounts, increased their Treasury holdings by +$20 billion and +$6 billion in August, to all-time highs of $491 billion and $448 billion, respectively.

China’s diversification away from the US Dollar may be slower than it appears.

posts.name: Nick Timiraos
posts.text: Warsh happened to take office just as the Fed turned toward tightening, which is when guidance has historically been more suited to heavy lifting. Guidance usually gets dated to 2008-09 and periods of ultra-accommodation, since the Fed obviously leaned on it aggressively at the zero lower bound. But its origins go back really to 1999 when officials wanted to take back the 1998 cuts without blindsiding markets the way the 1994 hikes had. So in May 1999 they did something new by issuing a policy statement at a meeting where they didn't move rates (previously, they only issued statements at meetings where they changed rates). They raised rates six weeks later (and the transcripts of May-99 show they realized a hike was very likely and they wanted to calibrate expectations). Officials didn't want to be misread.
